title: The reliability paradox: Why robust cognitive tasks do not produce reliable individual differences
institution: School of Psychology, Cardiff University (affiliation as printed); journal Behavior Research Methods (Springer)
description: Empirical methods paper. Three studies (50, 62 and 42 undergraduates recruited) measured the test-retest reliability, over two sessions three weeks apart, of seven classic tasks: Eriksen flanker, Stroop, stop-signal, go/no-go, Posner cueing, Navon and SNARC, using ICC(2,1) and the standard error of measurement. Reliabilities ranged from 0 to .82. The paper explains the paradox that tasks become robust and popular because between-participant variability is low, which is what makes them unreliable for individual differences; it decomposes variance, examines difference scores, corrects correlations for attenuation and discusses statistical power.

The OSF data repository was not opened.

Sections on difference scores, statistical power, cognitive neuroscience and clinical research, state dependence, other populations and future directions were seen as headings only; Table 1 was read in part and Tables 2-5 were not read.

The paper concerns reaction-time and error measures from seven attention and inhibition tasks, not learning-model parameters or bandit or planning tasks; applying its argument to fitted model parameters is an inference and must be stated as one.
